name: John Maynard Keynes
role: British economist, Liberal supporter and Bretton Woods negotiator (1883-1946)
summary: Keynes described himself as a liberal who rejected both laissez-faire and doctrinaire state socialism, wanting central control of money, credit and investment to secure full employment inside a market economy. He favoured graduated taxation, the 'euthanasia of the rentier', pacifism and arbitration, and opposed Bolshevism and totalitarian rule while stressing personal liberty and variety.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: In The General Theory ch. 24 he holds that once central controls secure full employment, private self-interest can decide what is produced and in what proportions, and that centralising decisions would not avoid errors of allocation.

public-ownership.rationale: In 'The End of Laissez-faire' he says big public-utility undertakings still need to be semi-socialised, preferably as semi-autonomous public corporations, while calling nationalisation of the railways a question of little importance.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The General Theory ch. 24 argues that growth does not depend on the savings of the rich, so one chief justification for great inequality is removed, and that some inequality is justified but not 'such large disparities as exist to-day'.

unions-good.rationale: He calls trade unionists 'once the oppressed, now the tyrants' whose sectional claims must be opposed, yet defends the miners against wage cuts and backs unions' resistance to being made victims of economic forces.

property-fundamental.rationale: He states that it is not true that individuals possess a prescriptive 'natural liberty' in economic activity and that no compact confers perpetual rights on those who have or acquire.

regulate-corporations.rationale: He wants society to exercise directive intelligence over private business, with legally required publicity of business facts and central control of credit, while leaving private initiative unhindered.

cut-welfare.rationale: In 1931 he attacked the Economy Committee's cuts to the dole and public pay as deflationary and unjust, though he also wanted the grave abuses of the dole reformed; he gives no dependency argument.

notes: Texts searched: Essays in Persuasion, General Theory, Economic Consequences of the Peace, Means to Prosperity, National Self-Sufficiency and three Lords speeches (1944-45). Themes searched: economy, taxation, trade, money, government form, peace and alliances, sex and drugs, population, technology. Eugenics Society roles were found but his own position on state action is not stated, so those statements stay null. Positions on tariffs and free trade shift between 1925, 1931-33 and 1944-45 and are recorded as mixed. O'Donnell (s9) reports continuity in his political philosophy over time.
